summary: Develops a threat model for attacks on Internet confidentiality, written after the 2013 revelations of pervasive surveillance. It assumes an attacker who wants undetected, indiscriminate eavesdropping, and it is based on published, verified attacks. It is a problem statement and not a set of solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine someone secretly reading everyone's mail. This note lists the ways that could happen online so people can plan how to stop it.

questions: what is the threat model for pervasive surveillance
how do attackers eavesdrop on internet traffic
what is a passive pervasive attack
subtitle: The IAB's catalogue of how an attacker with a view of much of the Internet can spy on traffic without being noticed.

tldr.problem: After the 2013 revelations of pervasive surveillance, the Internet community needed a precise description of the threats to confidentiality before it could decide what to fix.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an idealized passive attacker, adds the capabilities reported in published attacks, and sorts them into six attack classes with the costs and risks each one carries for the attacker.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement only: the Security Considerations section says mitigations are to be given in a future document.

facts.label: Idealized attacker
facts.value: Passive, observes every hop, takes no other action

sections.title: Why a Threat Model, and Key Terms
sections.content:
Starting in June 2013, documents released to the press revealed operations by intelligence agencies that exploited Internet communications. The attacks mostly used protocol vulnerabilities that were already known, but they were striking in both the volume of traffic targeted and the variety of techniques used.

The goal of RFC 7624 is to describe the threats more precisely and, from them, lay out the problems to be solved. It focuses on attacks that result in undetected eavesdropping, and it does not try to cover every possible attack.

A passive attack accesses a flow of packets without modifying it. An active attack modifies a flow. These words describe what the attacker does to the traffic, not how hard the attack is. A pervasive attack uses access at a large number of points in the network, or otherwise gets a large amount of traffic.

The RFC also separates an observation (information taken directly from communications, such as who sent an SMTP message to whom) from an inference (information derived by analysis, such as guessing which web page was fetched from flow sizes). A collaborator is a legitimate participant in a communication who gives information about it to the attacker, either deliberately or unwittingly. Key exfiltration and content exfiltration are the transfer of keys or content from a collaborator to the attacker.
sections.plainLanguage:
When people learned that someone was secretly listening in on lots of Internet traffic, engineers decided to write down exactly how that could work before trying to stop it.

Passive means just listening, like a person with a glass against the wall. Active means also changing what is said. A collaborator is someone in the conversation who tells the listener what they heard.

sections.title: The Idealized Passive Pervasive Attacker
sections.content:
The RFC starts from a deliberately limited attacker. It can observe every packet of all communications at any hop in any network path, can observe data at rest in any intermediate system, and can share information with other such attackers. It takes no other action: no blocking, modification or injection. The RFC notes that before 2013 these assumptions would have been considered on the border of paranoia outside the network security community.

Encryption is generally sufficient to prevent direct observation of content, assuming uncompromised implementations and keys. It gives less protection against inference. Even TLS-protected traffic exposes IP and TCP headers, including source and destination addresses and ports, and IPsec ESP still leaves IP addresses visible. DNS is a noted exception to the trend toward encrypted protocols, because DNSSEC does not have confidentiality as a requirement.

The RFC says there is little that can be done at protocol design time to limit correlation with outside data such as geolocation databases and social media.
sections.plainLanguage: Even if your letters are in sealed envelopes, the outside still shows who wrote to whom. A watcher can learn a lot from the envelopes alone.

sections.title: How Addresses Get Tied to People
sections.content:
Section 3.3 shows how the idealized attacker can link encrypted traffic to an individual. Each technique needs only one unprotected link in the chain.

  • IP headers: flow records built on the five-tuple of addresses, protocol and ports reveal which users use which services.
  • Identities: reverse DNS, or the cooperation of an ISP, can map an address to a user.
  • Messaging clients: POP3, IMAP and SIP often start with a password exchange, so a cleartext username is tied to a source address.
  • Mail headers: each SMTP relay adds a Received header, which can expose the submitting host's address and its NAT-internal address.
  • Web cookies: a cookie sent in cleartext lets the attacker link a new IP address to a known identity.
  • Graph analysis: addresses with similar usage patterns can be tied to the same person.
  • Link-layer identifiers: MAC addresses, and SSIDs probed by a device, can be used to track devices and their owners.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like following muddy footprints. Each footprint alone means little, but if one of them leads to your front door, the whole trail is yours.

sections.title: Reported Large-Scale Attacks
sections.content:
Reports on US and UK intelligence activity show that reality goes beyond the idealized attacker. The RFC cites examples including XKEYSCORE (searching for selectors such as email addresses), Tempora (access to around 1,500 major cables passing through the UK) and MUSCULAR (tapping cables between data centers). It also describes reported decryption efforts such as BULLRUN, direct access arrangements such as PRISM, and active techniques such as QUANTUM, which hijacks HTTP connections.

The RFC also mentions suspicion about modifications to the DUAL_EC_DRBG random number generator. It stresses that many organizations, most often nation-states, can mount such attacks, so legal limits in one jurisdiction cannot eliminate the risk. It points to China's Great Firewall as a system using techniques similar to QUANTUM.
sections.plainLanguage: The real spies turned out to be even more capable than the pretend one in the first example. They could tap huge numbers of cables and even try to weaken the locks.

sections.title: The Threat Model: Capabilities and Costs
sections.content:
The model has six attack classes. Passive observation directly captures data in transit. Passive inference infers from reduced or encrypted data. Active attacks manipulate or inject data. Three more rely on a collaborator: static key exfiltration (keys obtained once or rarely, such as a site operator handing over its HTTPS private key), dynamic key exfiltration (per-session key material, for example by predicting a compromised random number generator), and content exfiltration (access to data at rest, including history).

Each class carries a different cost and risk to the attacker, mainly the risk of discovery. Passive attacks risk discovery of the taps. Active attacks need more robust access and are more visible; a mis-issued certificate could be caught by Certificate Transparency. Static exfiltration is lower risk than dynamic because it needs only a few interactions with the collaborator. Content exfiltration needs a much higher bandwidth channel, which raises the chance of being found. The RFC also contrasts a full man-in-the-middle with a weaker man-on-the-side that can only inject or modify traffic at one point, such as sending TCP RST packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Some ways of spying are easy but easy to spot, like standing outside a window. Others need a helper on the inside, and every secret meeting with the helper is a chance to get caught.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section is a single statement: the document describes a threat model for pervasive surveillance attacks, and mitigations are to be given in a future document. The RFC therefore sets out the problem and leaves solutions to others.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper only lists the dangers. The answers are left for another day.
